clue.text: Mark of silver in the case of Holmes

definitions.meaning: a pale streak cut on a tree trunk, or the white stripe down a horse's face

definitions.text: of silver in the case of Holmes
definitions.meaning: Silver ___ is a Sherlock Holmes story about a missing racehorse

explanation.surface: A clue about a silver hallmark found during one of Sherlock Holmes's investigations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silver' looks like the metal, but it is the first half of a story title: 'Silver Blaze', in which Holmes hunts a stolen racehorse named for the white mark on its face.
explanation.definitionFit: A white streak on a horse's face is the standard term, and the racehorse in the Holmes tale is named after it.

clue.text: Setting for new clock in the City

indicators.note: the shuffled clock goes in the middle of the city's name

parts.note: Bath is the city in Somerset, England

indicators.note: new means the letters of clock are made into a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A setting is needed for a new clock in the City of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the City' suggests London's financial district, but here it is Bath, a city in Somerset; 'new' is the anagram signal and 'in' the container.
explanation.definitionFit: A painted cloth at the back of a stage, forming the scenery or setting.

clue.text: Topping recording worth copying

indicators.note: topping means cutting off the top, the first letter in a down entry

parts.note: taping is recording on tape

explanation.surface: A top-notch recording well worth copying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topping' looks like 'excellent' but means removing the head letter; 'worth' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Monkeys imitate, so to mimic someone is to copy them.

clue.text: Stop — amber — go in the right order

indicators.note: putting the words amber and go in the right order means rearranging their letters

explanation.surface: Traffic lights should run stop, amber, go in the proper sequence.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface lists traffic lights; 'Stop' is the definition, not a light.
explanation.definitionFit: An official ban on trade with a country, which stops it.

clue.text: Thrill to get going on a bike?

definitions.text: Thrill to get going on a bike?

parts.note: a kick is a thrill, as in 'getting a kick out of something'
to start is to get going

explanation.surface: A biker looks for an adrenaline rush to begin the ride.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines the word: a motorbike is started by kicking a pedal, and the two halves of the clue give the two halves of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Motorcycles were once fired up by stamping down on a lever, which is the literal sense; figuratively it means giving fresh momentum.

clue.text: As some would say, intricate

parts.note: a word meaning intricate or tangled, which in some accents is pronounced like a word for mischievous

explanation.surface: A remark that some people call something intricate.
explanation.walkthrough: In accents that drop the R, the word for intricate sounds like the word for badly behaved, which is what 'As some would say' hints at.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tangled with many knots is hard to unravel, hence complicated.

clue.text: Deceive over temporary housing for constituents

indicators.note: in a down clue over means the first piece sits on top of the second

parts.note: to con is to deceive
tents are temporary shelters

explanation.surface: Someone tricks constituents with promises of temporary homes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'constituents' suggests voters, but it means components.
explanation.definitionFit: The component parts of something are what it holds.

clue.text: One modest and secure in Shakespeare

definitions.text: One modest and secure in Shakespeare

parts.note: shy means modest, retiring
to lock is to secure

explanation.surface: Someone humble and safe found in Shakespeare's plays.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue points at a Shakespearean character; the moneylender in The Merchant of Venice is very keen to secure his bond.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jewish moneylender in The Merchant of Venice demanding his pound of flesh.

clue.text: Game bid is more than enough

definitions.meaning: in solo whist, a bid to win nine tricks

explanation.surface: In a card game, a bid that is overkill.
explanation.definitionFit: In the card game solo whist it is a call to take nine tricks; otherwise it means plenty.

clue.text: Formidable opponent of course from Asia

definitions.meaning: a fierce competitor, for instance on a golf course
the big striped cat native to Asia

explanation.surface: A dangerous rival naturally comes from Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' looks like 'naturally', but means on a golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: A fierce competitor is called by the name of the striped Asian big cat, also borne by the golfer Woods.

clue.text: Lower oneself in retreat

definitions.meaning: to descend, for instance from a ladder or rock face
a backing down from a position in an argument

explanation.surface: A climber abseils down while withdrawing from a mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally a descent on foot from a height; figuratively an embarrassing backing-off from a stated position.

clue.text: Novelist of the rising generation

definitions.meaning: Francis Brett ... or E. H. ..., English novelists
youthful, belonging to those now growing up

explanation.surface: A writer celebrated as the voice of a new generation.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Brett Young was an English novelist; youthful people are those of the generation now coming up.

clue.text: It helps to keep the weeds at bay

definitions.text: It helps to keep the weeds at bay

parts.words: It helps to keep the weeds at bay
parts.note: weeds is slang for cigarettes, and this device holds one away from the smoker's lips

explanation.surface: Apparently a garden tool or weedkiller that keeps unwanted plants away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weeds' suggests garden plants, but it is slang for cigarettes (or tobacco); the device holds the cigarette a little distance from the face.
explanation.definitionFit: A slim tube into which a smoker fits a cigarette, keeping the burning end at a distance.

clue.text: An indication of choice is possible in prayer

parts.note: the word or marks a choice between alternatives
taken as written
on means possible or feasible, as in 'that's not on'

explanation.surface: A remark that choosing remains possible when one prays.
explanation.walkthrough: ON for possible is the sense in 'is that plan on?'.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for a prayer, as in Hamlet's 'Nymph, in thy orisons'.

clue.text: In the last month no spirit of unseemliness

parts.note: taken as written
Dec is short for December, the last month of the year
O is nothing, zero
rum is a spirit

explanation.surface: Last December there was no improper drinking of spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Lack of propriety or good manners is improper behaviour.

clue.text: Crew has taken in fishing rig

indicators.note: the word taken is placed in the middle of the group word

parts.note: a set is a group or crew of people
taken as written

explanation.surface: A boat's crew has hauled in its fishing gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' is a link word; 'in' is the container signal, and 'Crew' must be read as a group of people.
explanation.definitionFit: A fishing net hung on stakes driven into the shore or seabed.

clue.text: Old theatres where charges could be daunting

definitions.text: Old theatres where charges could be daunting

parts.words: Old theatres where charges could be daunting
parts.note: medieval arenas where knights charged at each other with lances

explanation.surface: Historic playhouses whose ticket prices could scare off audiences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charges' suggests ticket prices, but means knights charging at each other in a joust; 'theatres' is used in the sense of arenas.
explanation.definitionFit: Enclosed grounds where medieval knights jousted, a kind of arena.

clue.text: No money and worried about being nicked

indicators.note: about means the worry word goes around the other letters

parts.note: cared means worried, as in 'cared about'
O is nothing, zero
L stands for pounds; doubled it stands for plural pounds, money

explanation.surface: Broke and anxious about getting arrested.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nicked' looks like stolen but is British slang for arrested. 'about' puts OLL inside CARED.
explanation.definitionFit: Grabbed by the collar, that is arrested; the definition's form describes being arrested.

clue.text: Boundary take over by nocturnal activist

parts.note: a hedge marks the boundary of a field
to hog is to take over and monopolise

explanation.surface: A night-time protester commandeers a field's boundary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' is a link; the definition is a playful description of an animal that forages at night.
explanation.definitionFit: This spiny mammal is active at night, snuffling in gardens for slugs and beetles.

clue.text: Permit to climb in the gloaming — dodgy?

indicators.note: the climbing permit is put in the middle of the evening word

parts.note: the gloaming is the dusk, evening, poetically eve

indicators.note: in a down clue climbing means reading upwards, so the permit runs backwards

parts.note: a visa is an entry permit

explanation.surface: A permit to go climbing at twilight seems suspicious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to climb' is the reversal signal in a down clue and 'in' the container; the gloaming is a Scots and poetic word for dusk.
explanation.definitionFit: Dodging a question is avoiding a straight answer, which is being slippery.

clue.text: To tell all could be a clever move — no copyright though

indicators.note: the letters of a clever are moved around to form a new word

explanation.surface: Telling everything might be smart strategy, though without copyright protection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no' and 'though' signal that C is taken out of A CLEVER before the remaining ALEVER is rearranged by 'move'.
explanation.definitionFit: To disclose a secret fully is to tell everything.

clue.text: Start work? It'S the way to force someone's hand

definitions.text: Start work? It'S the way to force someone's hand

parts.words: Start work? It'S the way to force someone's hand
parts.note: the opposite of starting work is finishing play; in bridge it is a technique that forces an opponent to lead

explanation.surface: Getting down to work is how to compel someone to act.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as a phrase it means stopping play, the opposite of 'Start work'; in bridge it is a manoeuvre near the end that forces an opponent into a losing lead.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridge technique where declarer throws an opponent into the lead to make them play to declarer's advantage.

clue.text: Lingered to avoid being frozen

definitions.meaning: wrapped in insulation, as pipes are against frost

explanation.surface: Someone loitered so as not to freeze.
explanation.definitionFit: To trail behind is to linger; pipes wrapped in insulation are protected from the frost.

clue.text: Term used by Lady Astor we hear

parts.note: Michaelmas is the autumn term at Oxford, Cambridge and the English law courts
Daisy is a woman's name

explanation.surface: A word that Nancy Astor, the first woman MP, might use.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on sound: 'Astor' said aloud is aster, the flower. Lady Astor was the first woman to sit in the British House of Commons.
explanation.definitionFit: This autumn-flowering plant is a species of aster, so it is an aster by sound.

clue.text: Coward found it extraordinarily potent when cheap

definitions.text: Coward found it extraordinarily potent when cheap

parts.words: Coward found it extraordinarily potent when cheap
parts.note: Noel Coward's line from Private Lives: 'Extraordinary how potent cheap ___ is'

explanation.surface: A timid person found something cheap remarkably strong, perhaps a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coward' looks like a timid person but is the playwright Noel Coward, quoted from Private Lives.
explanation.definitionFit: Coward's famous line praises popular songs, the tunes that stir feelings.

clue.text: Lay to rest in Tintern Abbey.

indicators.note: in signals that the letters sit inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A burial at Tintern Abbey, the ruined Welsh monastery.
explanation.walkthrough: Tintern Abbey is a ruined Cistercian abbey in Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: To bury a body is to lay it to rest in the ground.

clue.text: Raise rent for inn

indicators.note: rent means torn apart, so the letters of raise are ripped up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A landlord increases the rent at the inn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rent' looks like the landlord's charge but is the past tense of rend, torn.
explanation.definitionFit: A caravanserai, the roadside lodging for travellers in the Middle East and Central Asia.

clue.text: Governor demonstrates how a gun recoils before elevation

indicators.note: before places the first pieces ahead of the hill
recoils means springs backwards, so the gun's name runs back to front

parts.note: a Luger is a German pistol
a tor is a rocky hill or high point

explanation.surface: An official shows how a gun kicks back before rising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recoils' turns LUGER into REGUL; 'demonstrates how' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A governor in machinery is a device controlling speed, which is exactly a control mechanism of that name.

clue.text: Firm wound-up-members involved approved

indicators.note: the members are involved in, that is set within, the other pieces

parts.note: CO is short for company, a firm
wound up means finished, brought to an end
M stands for member, as in MP, so MM is members

explanation.surface: A company wound up after members got mixed up in approving it.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphenated 'wound-up' reads as tense, but it means finished; 'involved' is the container signal, setting the members between firm and finish.
explanation.definitionFit: To be praised officially is to receive a formal mark of approval.

clue.text: Bowls for the county

definitions.meaning: in cricket, to york a batsman is to bowl him with a yorker, a ball pitching at his feet
the standard short form of Yorkshire, a large English county

explanation.surface: Bowling for the county side, as a cricketer would.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link. A yorker is a cricket delivery aimed at the batter's feet; Yorkshire is a county in northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricketers say a bowler yorked a batsman; the abbreviation for Yorkshire appears in postal addresses.
